processing: As with other Wuyi rock teas: withered, shaken, partly oxidised, rolled and roasted.
harvest_season: Not recorded for this bush; Wuyi rock teas are normally picked in spring.
appearance_dry: Typical of Wuyi rock teas: dark, twisted strips.
appearance_liquor: Typical of roasted Wuyi oolongs: clear orange to amber.
appearance_wet: Typical of the class: green-brown leaves with darker edges.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting record exists for this bush. Expect what is typical of the class: roast, mineral depth and floral sweetness.

brewing.notes: The usual approach for Wuyi rock teas: water near the boil and short steeps.

vintage_note: Rarely seen on sale. If a lot does appear, expect the usual for Wuyi rock teas: labelled by spring harvest year and roast, in small quantity.
description:
Lü Dong Bin is a Wuyi famous-bush name, one of the long roll of over two hundred named bushes kept by the region's tea people. It shares its name with one of the Eight Immortals of Chinese folklore.

Little is documented about the bush itself. The making described here is that of the class: shaken, partly oxidised and roasted.

Expect the general shape of a Wuyi rock tea rather than a known signature flavour. Brew hot and short, and judge it on later steeps.

Any tea sold under this name deserves a question or two: which bush, which grower, which year. Similar names exist on Wuyi lists, including Dong Bin Cha and Zui Dong Bin, and it is not clear how they relate.
history: Little is documented beyond the name's place on lists of Wuyi famous bushes. A list of Qing-era names includes a Dong Bin Cha, but whether that is the same bush is not established.
